extracted.intended_audience: Unemployment Insurance Commission officials, policymakers, and claimant advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria governing how a Unemployment Insurance Commission identifies, notifies, classifies, recovers, and may write-off overpayments (recoupment, tax reversal, collection, garnishment, write-off). Includes timelines, letter content, discretion rules, and factors for assessing hardship or repayment ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overpayment categorization (A–G)
rubrics_metrics.description: All overpayments must be categorized under one of the following headings that provide capsule descriptions of causes of overpayment: A. earnings and employment; B. availability and capability; C. recomputation due to additional information; D. duplicate payments; E. renewal on non-renewable claim; F. inactive search for work; G. other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are referred to in UIC terminology as 'infractions' even where there may have been no claimant fault; categorization is the Commission's initial internal description of cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud/non-fraud classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Overpayments are classified as 'fraud' or 'non-fraud' depending on whether sec. 47 penalties or court costs have been assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification affects treatment of the overpayment and reflects an underlying presumption that overpayments are the claimant's responsibility; it influences recoupment, allowance of partial deductions, and write-off decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling by sex and marital status
rubrics_metrics.description: Overpayments are also labelled according to the sex and marital status of the claimant involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice supports informational requirements for certain collection methods (e.g., garnishment) and the UIC's assessment of the claimant's capacity to bear particular repayment methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification content and adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters informing claimants of overpayments should state the existence of an overpayment, describe its cause, and indicate how the UIC considers the amount can be repaid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual practice often omits telling claimants whether or how the decision can be appealed, that overpayments can result from UIC error, or about the full range of recovery methods and the Commission's discretion (e.g., reduced repayments, write-off). The pamphlets 'Rights and Obligations' and 'Appeal Procedure' may not adequately inform claimants of their options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoupment use and hardship consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Recoupment (deduction from subsequent benefits) is an authorized, commonly used recovery method that automatically reduces benefits payable until the overpayment is offset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although discretionary (s.49(3)), recoupment is treated as virtually automatic; officials may reduce the deduction if requested and claimant's finances indicate 'he requires a portion of his benefit to sustain himself'. Factors officials must consider include amount of overpayment, benefit payable, dependents, other financial commitments, and the cause (fraud may preclude partial deduction). Regional practices vary (e.g., minimum deduction 25% in some regions; HQ indicated lower rates may become national standard). There is a proposal to delay recoupment for two weeks for non-fraud cases to allow negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax reversal application and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax reversal converts income tax credits deducted at source into repayments of overpayments (accessing tax credits in the calendar year) and is automatically applied for non-active claimants where tax credits are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training in some regions directs that tax reversal should be used 'as often as possible' for non-active overpayments; UIC usually applies it automatically and individuals are informed only that income tax deductions are being applied. UIC typically does not consider individual's capacity to cope with tax reversal nor uniformly publicize options (such as voluntary repayment agreements that might prevent reversal). Tax reversal repays the actual amount paid to the claimant (avoids gross-up issues present in other recovery methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write-off authority and criteria (reg. 175)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may declare amounts 'no longer due and owing' (write-off) when, having regard to all the circumstances, (i) the sums are uncollectable, or (ii) repayment would result in undue hardship to the claimant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write-offs are also possible for trivial amounts (e.g., $5 or less), death, discharge in bankruptcy, etc. The discretion to write off is broad and the Commission has not uniformly publicized this power; write-off decisions terminate liabilities established by the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection procedures, responsibilities and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection encompasses actions (other than recoupment and tax reversal) to achieve repayment for inactive accounts: locating the debtor, arranging voluntary repayments, garnishment, and Federal Court enforcement. District collection units normally have 90 days (or less at a region's option) to collect outstanding amounts before regional review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some regions centralize collection in regional units; exceptions to the 90-day limit include amounts of $25 and under, voluntary agreements being honored, and district-initiated garnishments. If a new claim is established, district responsibility ceases and recoupment becomes appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary collection communications and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: District collection units follow a standard sequence of form letters and contact attempts: initial special form letter; if no response after 14 days, telephone attempts and interview requests; if two days of efforts fail, a second (blunter) letter; a further two weeks without response triggers a third (blunt) letter threatening referral to 'collection experts' and other action unless payment within ten days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These letters are not tailored to case circumstances by default, and do not inform debtors of write-off or undue hardship possibilities. An appeal of the underlying decision postpones further collection letters for 30 days to await appeal outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary repayment agreement assessment factors and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection officials may accept instalment arrangements but must use 'good judgment on the debtor's ability to repay' and consider: monetary resources; domestic responsibilities and other commitments; amount outstanding; negligence in earlier repayments; and cause of the overpayment (fraud involved?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials are told to watch collection costs, keep repayment periods short relative to amounts and 'current circumstances', avoid instalments extending beyond two years, be aware of statutory limitation periods, and treat NSF cheques as non-compliance. If debtor becomes eligible for benefits, agreed weekly repayments usually continue unless the overpayment was caused by fraud. Once writ of execution issued, instalments may no longer be authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debtor locating practices and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: When existing information is inadequate, collection officials may use commercial credit information services to locate ex-claimants and gather employment and financial information (addresses, last known employment, income, assets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials are instructed not to reveal information in credit reports to the people concerned and not to publicize that the UIC uses commercial agencies for collection purposes. Asset assessments from these agencies inform decisions such as Federal Court action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garnishment prerequisites and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Garnishment (sec. 80 applied to overpayment collection) is used 'with great discretion' typically when the person is employed, employer known, and the amount exceeds $25; it may also be used against other income and bank accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements for initiating garnishment include: the 'debtor' has been clearly notified of the reason for indebtedness and his right to appeal; all usual and reasonable means of communication (letters, telephone, personal interviews at a minimum) have been exhausted; and consideration that the person is 'financially capable' and will not voluntarily accept a mutually agreeable settlement. Officials are instructed to give 'due regard' to personal circumstances and the potential harm to reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad discretionary authority of UIC in overpayment treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC has broad discretion under the Act and Regulations in deciding whether repayment ought to occur at all, whether amounts should be written off, and which recovery methods to use (recoupment, tax reversal, garnishment, court enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although policies and procedures structure discretion somewhat, regional and district officials exercise significant judgment in applying methods; criteria for exercising methods give fairly broad latitude to determine the burden a method will impose and whether a lesser burden would be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-conscious and time-limited collection policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection officials are instructed to watch collection costs and keep repayment periods short relative to amounts and 'current circumstances'; avoid instalment arrangements beyond two years and be aware of statutory limitation periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constraints inform decisions on acceptance of voluntary agreements, escalation to garnishment or Federal Court, and whether amounts under certain thresholds should be pursued vigorously or written off after time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repayment amount calculation depends on recovery method
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount an individual must repay varies by recovery method: tax reversal repays the actual amount paid to the claimant (using tax credits), while other recovery methods generally require repayment of the gross amount including tax deducted at source (the UIC recovers tax from the person rather than the Department).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difference can make tax reversal preferable to some claimants because it avoids an initial out-of-pocket payment of tax until the claimant's tax return is processed; UIC practices on deferring tax portion repayment until tax return are not uniformly applied or publicized.
